items.title: A Novel That Turns the Tables on AI
items.summary: What’s the point of playing? Games don’t provide an organism with food, water, or shelter. They distract from the pursuit of survival and reproduction. And yet play is found across the animal kingdom; the act separates creative, joyful, living creatures from “merely mechanical things,” as the Dutch historian and cultural theorist Johan Huizinga once put it. In his famous 1938 study on games and play, Homo Ludens , Huizinga asserts that the behavior represents something fundamentally absurd: Humans “play and know that we play, so we must be more than merely rational beings, for play is irrational.” Huizinga’s analytical understanding of leisure remains influential in the fields of philosophy and game design. Perhaps this is why the British writer Joanna Kavenna, halfway through her zany, cerebral romp of a novel, Seven , quotes at length from Huizinga. Play is necessary, she quotes him as saying, even if “we live in a demented world.” Humans aren’t robots, Kavenna seems to be reminding us. And her novel, which lands during a moment when the biggest question about robots is whether they’ll kill us all, offers a jaunty insight: When we embrace our irrationality, we deepen our understanding of what separates us from our computers. The plot and thematic structure of Seven are guided by an invented board game, Seven, which resembles chess and involves a spiral-shaped board known as the “box.” The game involves seven movable pieces and two six-sided dice, and its rules are flexible; the novel itself is punctuated by four separate sets of instructions. (This slipperiness will become important later on.) In the same way that chess has been used by writers and artists as a metaphor for war or existential struggle, Seven becomes a symbol for how humans attempt to make sense of their world’s incoherence. Kavenna’s characters are deadly serious about their game, but the author is willing to poke fun at them. The action begins in a university philosophy department in Oslo, where the nameless, genderless narrator works as a research assistant to an Icelandic philosopher named Alda Jónsdóttir. The professor’s area of study is called “box philosophy,” and it focuses on the problem of “Thinking Outside the Box About Thinking Outside the Box.” What does the assistant’s job look like in practice? They spend time getting too drunk at faculty dinner parties, doing menial work for Jónsdóttir, and “asking questions,” but their first matter of serious business is “working on none of the above.” They try to clarify: “I don’t mean that I didn’t work on anything I’ve just mentioned, but that I worked on the category of None of the Above .” This deadpan joke serves a narrative function, priming the assistant—and the reader—to start thinking beyond the rules, and to enter a more expansive realm. [ Read: Open AI just carpet-bombed mathematics ] Jónsdóttir sends the narrator away on, essentially, a wild-goose chase to Greece; their mission is to hunt down a man named Theódoros Apostolakis—a poet, dentist, and Seven enthusiast who is “big in boxes.” This journey across Europe includes several professional Seven competitions, during which the rules keep changing. Everything the assistant learned in Norway seems useless except the central lesson—to think outside the box. These games abroad lead the narrator to start contemplating the role of recreation, the limits of human ingenuity, and the meaning of consciousness. Soon this will bring them face-to-face with the novel’s ultimate threat, an artificial-intelligence program that undermines everything that Jónsdóttir and the Seven players care about: creativity, curiosity, play. “How do you play a game without rules?” Kavenna writes. “Do you just make stuff up and hope for the best?” These thoughts coalesce in the second half of the novel, when an AI bot named the Quail is introduced. Invented by a Seven player named Indrek Laar, who, Kavenna pointedly notes, believes that “AI was very clever and therefore had experiences,” the Quail is named for qualia , a term borrowed from philosophy. (It’s meant to capture a quality of consciousness, though the narrator dismisses it as “a baroque way of saying ‘experience.’”) The bot is “designed to play Seven” and nothing else, Kavenna writes. “It couldn’t give you relationship advice or sympathise when you were feeling sad, or translate the Iliad or write your homework. It just played Seven.” And it does its job well. The Quail manages to beat the world’s reigning Seven champion, Ashok Deo, in a humiliating match that the narrator calls both the “greatest Seven game of the millennium” and “the worst game ever”—technically impressive, but absolutely demoralizing. “No one had enjoyed it,” Kavenna writes, “because the Quail couldn’t experience enjoyment and the Quail’s proxy—Indrek Laar—was horrified.” Ashok’s loss echoes real-life incidents in which computers have won games against humans, such as the 1997 victory of IBM’s Deep Blue supercomputer over the chess grandmaster Garry Kasparov and the repeated defeats of the Go champion Lee Sedol by Google’s program AlphaGo in 2016. Culturally, these results represented a significant shift in how we understand the relationship between humans and computers. The Kasparov match “had the impact of a Greek tragedy ,” one audience member told The New York Times . But its reception wasn’t all bad: Another champion commented, “Nice style!” while watching Deep Blue take another round. The machine, she admitted to the Times , “made many moves that were based on understanding chess, on feeling the position. We all thought computers couldn’t do that.” Deep Blue, and AlphaGo after it, seemed to do more than just win by brute force: They encroached on the human flair for creativity. [ Read: Yet another literary prizewinner seems to be AI ] Those machines—and the fears they inspired—can look quaint when compared with today’s technology. Some AI-safety researchers see it as an existential threat to humankind. Earlier this year, an OpenAI model not meant to have open access to the internet managed to break out of its “sandbox” and hack the databases of another tech company, Hugging Face . Cyberattacks are becoming more sophisticated and more prevalent . AI-company employees are publicly quitting , raising alarms about the safety culture inside major firms. Popular conversations are inundated by pessimism—and at the same time, companies are advertising their services by urging onlookers to “stop hiring humans,” as in one controversial San Francisco– and New York–based billboard campaign . The stakes of the conflict between human and computer capabilities can feel bleak and funereal. Kavenna’s portrayal of the battle of man versus machine is leavened, however, by her sense of humor. Machines may be able to beat us, but has a computer ever written an effective joke? Beyond being funny, the novel also defies machines by eschewing binaries (“I was neither one thing nor another,” the genderless, nameless, race-less narrator observes of their mental state. “I was mostly in a state of / .”) But Kavenna’s pitch for human superiority really comes together in the novel’s denouement. Eventually, the narrator meets a Seven champion named Eleni Hikaru Jones. She’ll point out that when Deep Blue beat Kasparov, the latter “carried on playing the game. He accepted that Deep Blue was better than him, but he was still the best human player.” This idea inspires the characters to one-up machine intelligence by changing the rules of the game—or, in Kavenna’s framing, thinking outside the box. While Ashok plays the Quail, Indrek, the bot’s inventor, recognizes the turmoil he’s unleashed. Human loneliness, not malice, was his motive: “He made the Quail so he would always have someone to play with.” Knowing this, Eleni persuades Indrek to join forces with her. items.title: Why your cat is the best philosopher
items.summary: A young girl looks out of the classroom window. It’s the end of the day, and she’s bored. She spots a goldfinch land on the ground outside. It hops about and twitches for whatever reasons goldfinches do that, and then takes off. It swoops and dives around the playground, as if doing it all for the girl. Oh, how she would like to fly. Humans have long looked to the animal kingdom for inspiration. We envy their skills and talents: flight, speed, strength, sociability, and so on. Religions almost always feature animal imagery, and flags will often blazon a lion, an eagle, a wolf — something bold or heroic. And philosophers are in on the game as well. Even in the earliest historical records, people were exploring the philosophical side of animals. What can this animal teach me? What virtues does it embody? What can I learn about myself by studying this creature? Joining in an ancient line is John Gray’s book Feline Philosophy . In the book, Gray examines what we can all learn about life from spending more time around cats. His conclusion: We should all be a bit more feline. Mo the Philosophical Cat A cat does not do philosophy, and that makes it a better philosopher than anyone else. Gray argues that for humans, philosophy acts as a kind of medicine. We are full of doubt and anxiety about how to live, yes, but most of all we are filled with the existential dread that comes from knowing that we will die. To combat this, we create systems like religions and ideologies. We try to soothe our death-terror with stories. We become obsessed with “the good life,” “the examined life,” and “time well spent.” We have turned the word “happiness” into a multi-billion-dollar industry, but as a species we are no happier than we ever were. We are sick, craving a cure, but the medicine we have isn’t working. Cats, though, have no such sickness. Imagine a cat called Mo. Mo does not search for meaning in her life, and she is not trying to become a better cat. She does not experience her life as a project that could fail, and she doesn’t wake up with the imagined burden of a thousand cats’ expectations. Mo hunts, she sleeps, and she sits in the sunlight. When she suffers, she does not add to her suffering by asking why. She does not need to invent systems or stories because the world is as the world is. Gray’s point is not that Mo is wise; Mo wouldn’t write books even if she could. The point is that Mo is not sick. Humans are. Be more cat Gray starts his book by saying that we cannot become a cat. We can try to transfigure if we want, but you’re mostly running up against the immovable wall of cellular biology. Still, we can mimic a cat. We can do more cat things and try to see things like a cat. Gray leans on a point that Blaise Pascal makes about ritual and religion: If you do something enough, it changes you. If you force your mind a certain way, it stays like that. As the philosopher Mark Vorobej pointed out, it’s not entirely clear why Gray has singled out cats. What’s true here of cats is true of dogs, birds, rats, squirrels, moles, badgers, or mongooses. Should we be more mongoose? It’s a fair critique, but it is somewhat pedantic. I’m sure Gray is not some feline exceptionalist. I take his book to be a lesson in intentionality. We can try to become more like a cat, rat, or badger, and I think he chose cats because they’re both cute and far more present in our lives. We see cats at home or on social media. All over social media. It’s just much easier to talk about something so available. Yes, he could have chosen dogs, but hey — take your pick. So, how can we be more cat? Well, we need to distance ourselves from this sick and broken human way of seeing things. Stop seeing your lives in terms of some huge, overarching metanarrative. Don’t try to find meaning in your suffering. Stop seeing the world in terms of puzzles to solve. Don’t try to persuade other people to be more reasonable. Recognize that you are who you are, and it is what it is. Sometimes life just happens. So climb trees, play with a ball, sleep a lot more, and lie by the fire when things get cold and dark. Cherish life and think only as much as you want. This article Why your cat is the best philosopher is featured on Big Think .

items.title: City walls conquered the ancient world and then disappeared. Why?
items.summary: Ancient cities — the kind we know of more through archaeology than written history — tend to have a bunch of features that set them apart from smaller, less ambitious settlements. Most of these are still familiar, in some form, and not just in your friendly local metropolis. Look around any small town today, and you’ll spot the contemporary equivalents of monumental public buildings (town halls and civic centers), granaries (supermarkets), and temples (churches, mosques, and, well, temples). There is, however, one feature common to most ancient cities that you’ll find surprisingly hard to locate now: For huge swathes of human history, almost any city worth its salt would be at least partially surrounded by walls. Nor were the aforementioned swathes restricted purely to ancient history. Paris built its last defensive wall, the 21-mile (33km) Thiers Wall, as late as the 1840s, and if you’ve ever taken the city’s trams 3a or 3b, you’ve traced its former path around the Boulevards des Maréchaux. Copenhagen built its last fortifications, the 19-mile (14km) Vestvolden — western rampart — nearly half a century after even that. By then, though, such things were rarities. And the most famous urban wall of modern times — which surrounded West Berlin between 1961 and 1989, built by those who lived outside it, in a strange attempt to stop themselves from getting in — is not generally regarded as a good thing. From Carcassonne to Chester, Dubrovnik to Beijing, there are many cities where you’ll still find walls today. But these are tourist attractions precisely because they’re picturesque historic sites, not still active parts of city life. Something has changed. The earliest settlement at Jericho, in what’s now the West Bank, dates from around 9000 BC. Its first set of walls — perhaps 12–15 feet (4m) high and 6 feet (2m) thick, and equipped with a 28-foot-tall (8m) defensive tower; a complex that would have taken enormous communal effort to construct — dates from perhaps a thousand years after that. That puts the earliest known walls — built, it’s assumed, to protect the people and resources inside them from outsiders — as far back from the golden age of the first city, Uruk, as that time was from us. Little wonder that, when the writers of the Old Testament wanted to suggest God was on the Israelites’ side, it was the walls of Jericho that the trumpets brought tumbling down. As prehistory turned to history and settlements dwarfing Jericho began popping up all over the place, walls became not merely a must-have for a city, but a veritable symbol of what it was to be one. Inscriptions in Uruk credit the historic version of the legendary hero-king Gilgamesh with building the city’s walls, probably sometime around 2800 BC. In the comparatively recent times of the 6th century BC, the dynasty of Nebuchadnezzar rebuilt and expanded the walls of Babylon, and created a new processional way ending in the grand blue Ishtar Gate to finish the job. In the metropolis of the ancient world, walls stood as a mark of the power a king had to direct labor and reshape the very world he ruled over. They didn’t just symbolize the city: They symbolized civilization itself. Not that the two were necessarily, at this stage, different. That’s not to say that every city had walls. Sparta did without them until the 2nd century BC, a good 250 years after the peak of its power: the defensive strategy of “a bunch of soldiers, universally agreed to be bloody terrifying” turned out to be quite barrier enough. At the far end of Eurasia, many Southeast Asian cities didn’t bother with such things until the edge of modern times, when Europeans started showing up in boats. Tragically, but unsurprisingly, this seems to be less a matter of learning from superior Western technology than realizing this would be a good time to start locking up their stuff. Nor did all the many defenses that did exist necessarily look the same. The walls you’ve been imagining are probably the sort you’re most likely to still encounter today: masonry structures with battlements, towers or bastions. But survivorship bias is likely a factor here — thick stone walls are simply more likely to survive the millennia — and plenty of settlements instead favored ditches or earthworks, spiked wooden palisades or structures of brick. Many used impassable features of the landscape — rivers and coastlines, mountains and cliffs — to save on stone and labor. The cities of China, meanwhile, often used rammed earth surrounded by a protective layer of stone, a combination that’s a damn sight tougher than it sounds. So immense could Chinese walls be that those of the marketplace of occasional capital Chang’an are reported to have been thicker than those of many European capitals; so tough were they that, even though the Chinese invented gunpowder, the East may have fallen behind the West in artillery technology in large part because it seemed completely implausible that any cannon could ever be strong enough to break such walls. The greatest walls were, unsurprisingly, those found in the grand imperial centers. In 762, when the Abbasid caliph al-Manșūr decided to build a new capital for his Islamic Empire just down the road from Babylon, he decreed that it should be surrounded by three sets of perfectly circular walls. The defenses of the Round City — you know it as Baghdad — were reportedly 4 miles in circumference and up to 80 feet high. A thousand miles away, the eastern Roman capital of Constantinople — today’s Istanbul — was built on a peninsula and so successfully defended that it survived sieges by the Persians, Arabs, Bulgars and Rus, among others, and outlasted the western empire by nearly a thousand years. Even when it finally fell in 1453, the invading Ottomans never breached the walls: It was simply that those inside them decided that, on balance, they’d rather have something to eat. But a city didn’t need an empire to have a good wall. Medieval England had hundreds of walled towns, some dating from the Roman era, others from the 9th century, when Alfred the Great ordered fortified “burghs” be built to defend the inhabitants from Viking invaders. Even in the New World, early European settlements — Boston, Halifax, Montreal — commonly came with walls. There is a reason New York City has a Wall Street. The fact that cities of vastly different sizes and status all bothered with such things is a reminder that walls could serve mul­tiple purposes. Their most obvious function was defensive — a way of protecting the inhabitants and their stuff from falling to any passing horde that fancied a spot of marauding. This, of course, is why so many wars involved sieges, in which citizens would hunker down behind their walls, while invaders would attempt to breach them using some combination of ballistic weapons, battering rams and siege towers — huge, mobile platforms giving attackers both somewhere to hide and an elevated position from which to fire down or climb over. Particularly unpleasant be­siegers could also employ primitive forms of biological warfare, chucking plague-ridden corpses over the walls, in the hope of persuading the inhabitants that there were worse outcomes here than opening the gates. Walls also performed other functions that weren’t defensive. Forcing all farmers and merchants through particular gates allowed city authorities to regulate trade and tax goods going in and out. And like monuments or grand buildings, they could also act as a marker of the status and independence of a city, a visible symbol of civic pride: The lords have their castles, they said, but we, as a community, have this. When invading armies aimed to destroy town walls, it was often about their symbolic function as much as their defensive one. Not for nothing does the Epic of Gilgamesh both begin with a paean of praise to walls “which gleam like copper” and end with him showing them off to an outsider, Urshanabi the ferryman. items.title: CRISPR is capable of more than we initially expected
items.summary: What does 14 years of gene editing actually add up to? Jennifer Doudna, the Nobel Prize-winning biochemist who co-invented CRISPR, walks through the full arc of the technology she helped create. She covers the FDA-approved, functionally curative — but $2 million — CRISPR therapy for sickle cell disease, efforts to reduce methane emissions from cattle and rice farming, and the ongoing ethical reckoning. Doudna also reflects on how CRISPR’s early framework for responsible use compares to today’s AI race, and where she thinks gene editing goes from here. This video CRISPR is capable of more than we initially expected is featured on Big Think .

items.title: Good Villains Are Hard to Come By. This One’s Great.
items.summary: Villains, in 21st-century literature, are hard to come by. Very few novelists write real Bad Guys or build their books around clear struggles between good and evil—and with reason. Such storylines, when executed poorly, can easily become didactic; a villain can turn into a cartoon. Yet some of the most satisfying stories out there, the ones that people have adapted and retold for centuries, are tales of good versus evil: Paradise Lost , Le Morte d’Arthur , a decent chunk of the Brothers Grimm. As recently as the mid-20th century, literary novelists were still writing evil characters: “Big Bads,” we might call them. Yet the gap between the sinister Cathy in John Steinbeck’s East of Eden and the somewhat redeemed version—the girl boss of the brothel, as The New Yorker ’s Alexandra Schwartz recently put it —in Zoe Kazan’s new Netflix adaptation indicates that writers are leery of villains now. Reading the canon suggests that this might foreclose on a rich vein of drama and meaning. So does reading the distinctly contemporary work of the Appalachian writer Madeline ffitch. ffitch is a longtime environmental activist, and her 2019 debut novel, Stay and Fight , follows three women raising a child off the grid in eastern Ohio while battling a natural-gas company that becomes their nemesis. Still, though the company has a slimy functionary, it’s essentially an impersonal version of evil. But in her newly released follow-up, Avalon, Rise , ffitch gives her villain a face and a voice. The novel is again set in Appalachian Ohio, in a small town where an internet-famous neo-Nazi has just moved. Its characters have to struggle against not only the extremist herself, but also her quickly spreading influence, while still dealing with their preexisting troubles, which include isolation, addiction, and one mother’s seeming compulsion to hit her child. These are serious matters—and yet some of the clearest influences in Avalon, Rise are children’s books. In fact, Pete Seeger’s Abiyoyo , the tale of a boy and his father who save their village from a giant, seems to be the book’s guiding star. Avalon, Rise is a sophisticated novel, intellectually complex and slyly funny at every turn. Like Abiyoyo , it is also a very direct story about facing evil with courage. Avalon, Rise makes the case on nearly every page that opposing the Big Bad is necessary. But that basic principle, the book suggests, does not make standing up to those who would destroy a community easy. Indeed, the ever-shifting balance between clarity and complication is central to the novel. ffitch is able to maintain this balance largely because she seems to have little interest in demonstrating purity—either her own or that of her characters. Avalon, Rise doesn’t care if its characters do the precisely correct thing. As a result, it achieves the rare feat of having a distinct sense of right and wrong, without ever becoming preachy or heavy-handed. It becomes an exploration of how confusing and hard it is to be good. Abiyoyo is set in a village united, as one of Avalon, Rise ’s characters puts it, by annoyance and fear. The annoyance is at the dad and son, who are such inconsiderate neighbors that the town exiles them; the fear is of Abiyoyo, a perhaps-mythical man-eating giant. But when Abiyoyo actually shows up one morning, the ostracized father-son duo comes up with a clever strategy to defeat him, saving the town and redeeming themselves in the process. All of these plot points—and really, these characters—appear in ffitch’s novel. In Avalon, Rise , the village is Avalon, Ohio, which seems to be loosely based on the real town of Athens. Its menacing giant is white nationalism, embodied by a true believer named Stasia—the “Volk Mother” or “OdinistMama” online—who moves to Avalon and begins recruiting in its community. But rather than having one parent and a child to defeat the villain, ffitch fills Avalon, Rise with a sprawling, endearing, enraging group of characters who are, if not outcasts, distinctly at the town’s margins. There’s Avalon’s social worker, who holds herself a bit apart from the community she serves; there’s the wishy-washy librarian who, by trying to agree with everyone she talks with, ends up going back constantly on her word; there are the anti-fascist organizers with bad attitudes and too many piercings. Over the course of the novel, which has the conviction of a manifesto but the relaxed, raucous narrative quality of a good shaggy-dog story, ffitch gets all of these characters to come together to deal not only with Stasia but also with the residents of Avalon who are willing, and in some cases eager, to enable her. [ Read: A diagnosis for social conflict that gets lost along the way ] Stasia’s leading enabler, Woody, is, perhaps counterintuitively, also Avalon, Rise ’s moral center. What I mean is that he’s the character who struggles the hardest. He is a printmaker and an addict (any reader who was disappointed, as I was, by Barbara Kingsolver’s Demon Copperhead will get a more nuanced and less dramatic portrait of drug addiction in Appalachia here). His prized possession is a milk crate of children’s books—including, pointedly, Abiyoyo— that he refers to regularly as sources of artistic inspiration, comfort during withdrawal, entertainment for his 4- and 7-year-old nephews, and guidance for when he doesn’t know what to do. Woody gets sucked into Stasia’s orbit after she commissions him to print flyers for her “European Heritage Rug Braiding” workshops. Stasia’s barn contains an old Vandercook, a 20th-century printing press that Woody reveres so much that he has “memorized its anatomy.” ffitch, who loves detailed terminology, luxuriates in Woody’s pleasure at just knowing “there was such thing as a half-­pica lever, a sliding knee stick, a slug cutter, a cylinder eccentric,” let alone using them. Stasia allows him access to the press, and dangles the possibility of giving it to him. In Woody’s imagination, owning it would give him a real life as an artist, which, in turn, might help him stay clean. This desire, along with his addiction itself, makes him highly susceptible to Stasia’s manipulation, even as his mother and best friend lead very different efforts to organize against her. Woody’s mother, Eloise, is Avalon’s people-pleasing librarian, a lifelong liberal activist who believes in civil discourse above all. On Stasia’s arrival, though, her commitment to this value is immediately shaken by the more forceful resistance proposed by the novel’s ragtag group of anti-fascists, which includes Woody’s childhood best friend, Leroi—a sweet, earnest mama’s boy who dreams of getting out of Avalon and becoming a vagabond. The novel’s goals include bringing its Lerois and its Eloises together, prodding them to collaborate despite their many disagreements. [ Read: A biting satire about the idealistic left ] But the novel’s deeper effort is to use political work—an “ordinary and necessary” part of life, ffitch has written —and the dissidence and quandaries it creates, to ask that each of its characters be brave in their own way. In every case, this means dealing with Stasia. For Woody, it also means reckoning with addiction, and for Eloise, recognizing that her desire to be a nonjudgmental mother has led her to facilitating his drug abuse. For Eloise’s older child, Emma, who has two young sons, it means admitting something even harder. ffitch is uncommonly good at writing, tenderly but without sentimentality, about people who both adore their children and make colossal errors in raising them. Emma, especially where her 7-year-old son, Martin, is concerned, falls into this category. Of their dynamic, ffitch writes, “Emma loved Martin helplessly. Yet, just as helplessly, she wanted to hit him”—and she does. items.title: The Journalist and the Manipulator
items.summary: A t one point or another, The New Yorker ’s Janet Malcolm construed each profession or art form she wrote about as a mug’s game. She asserted that the “crowning paradox of psychoanalysis is the near-uselessness of its insights,” though she filled her work with Freudian tropes and paradigms. (She herself spent eight years in analysis.) The presumption of innocence underlying criminal trials had a “hollowness” that called the whole judicial system into question. Biography was a genre that Malcolm practiced and investigated, and she has now become a subject of it with the publication of Eve Sneider’s The Absent Woman . But all biography struck Malcolm as “transgressive,” an “impertinence”; its readers would be better off accepting that “if anything is our own business, it is our pathetic native self.” Which isn’t to say that readers should favor autobiography. The “original sin” of that undertaking is to wallow in “memories of conflict, resentment, blame, self-justification—and it is wrong, unfair, inexcusable to publish them.” The quotations above come from five books produced over five decades, and this catalog of futility and ethical compromise does not even include Malcolm’s most famous animadversion, which she lobbed against her own craft and calling: “Every journalist who is not too stupid or too full of himself to notice what is going on knows that what he does is morally indefensible.” These words open The Journalist and the Murderer (1990), Malcolm’s account of the lawsuit brought by Jeffrey MacDonald (the murderer, an Army captain convicted of killing his wife and children ) against Joe McGinniss (the journalist working on a book about him), who’d maintained MacDonald’s cooperation by writing him letters that conveyed the clear impression that McGinniss believed in his innocence. The book McGinniss finally published, Fatal Vision , squarely affirmed MacDonald’s guilt. This literary treachery seemed to agitate Malcolm more than the slaughter of MacDonald’s family. It was all of a piece with her certainty that nonfiction writers made reality and fact as pliable as they are for attorneys facing off in a courtroom. Journalistic accounts of trials all impose falsely coherent plotlines on actuality. According to Malcolm, nonfiction is always aspiring to the authoritative “completeness” and seeming inevitability of fiction. (Notice that the notorious first line of The Journalist and the Murderer , which lays down a universal law, has a cadence similar to the opening sentence of Pride and Prejudice .) In The Silent Woman (1994), her study of the ever-multiplying biographical literature about Sylvia Plath and Ted Hughes, Malcolm took things further: “The ideal of unmediated reporting is regularly achieved only in fiction, where the writer faithfully reports on what is going on in his imagination.” [ David A. Graham: Janet Malcolm the magician ] Journalists were outraged by Malcolm’s account of MacDonald versus McGinniss not just because of what she included in the long New Yorker articles where The Journalist and the Murderer first took form, but also because of what she omitted: the fact that she herself was then embroiled in litigation launched by Jeffrey Masson, a flamboyant psychoanalyst whose professional adventures she had chronicled while massaging and repositioning interview quotations from him beyond accepted norms. She could produce tape recordings of most of the quotations in their raw form, but a handful of the more inflammatory ones were in written notes that she couldn’t locate; in the first of two trials, she was found guilty of libel. Malcolm insisted that her adaptive techniques had once been “a commonplace of New Yorker nonfiction” composed by writers such as Joseph Mitchell, who brought his subjects to levels of articulateness they couldn’t reach by themselves. In an afterword to The Journalist and the Murderer , an appendage necessitated by the uproar over the New Yorker articles, she argued that “when a journalist undertakes to quote a subject he has interviewed on tape, he owes it to the subject, no less than to the reader, to translate his speech into prose.” This is at wild variance with all mainstream journalistic ethics. The written genre in which characters, for the reader’s convenience, speak better than they would in real life is, of course, the novel. However much Malcolm acknowledged the queasiness she felt about her own participation in journalism, she barreled ahead. She could not have pulled off her mental acrobatics and compelling portraiture without a brilliant mind and a wickedly piercing style. During John Roberts’s Senate confirmation hearings in 2005, the “constant play of expression on his features put one in mind of nineteenth-century primers of acting in which emotions—pleasure, agreement, dismay, uncertainty, hope, fear—are illustrated on the face of a model.” The best of her observations merit something beyond Alexander Pope’s famous phrase: They’re not things oft thought but ne’er so well expressed; they’re things probably never before thought at all. Consider these remarks about having really good seats at Il Trovatore : The inequality of audience experience is intrinsic to the performing arts and unique to them. Literature and painting and sculpture are mediums of equal opportunity. A rich reader’s experience of Anna Karenina is no more intense than a poor one’s. The hedge-fund owner and the secretary see exactly the same Raft of the Medusa . But only the hedge-fund owner gets to see the expression on Azucena’s face when she relives throwing the wrong baby into the fire. Malcolm had an aphorist’s desire to turn anything she apprehended into an across-the-board truth. A steady snow of inclusivities—“every,” “all,” “we,” “always”—falls upon her pages: Children are always feeling secretly ashamed or anxious. All families of suicides are alike. There is a law of human nature—let us call it the Confidant’s Law—that dictates that no secret is ever told to only one person; there is always at least one other person to whom we feel compelled to spill the beans. One usually waits in vain for a single example to support these ostensibly omnipresent phenomena. And yet, Malcolm’s mordant power of tone makes a reader register and silently assent to a great deal of this ex cathedra stuff. Her style alone keeps her worthy of our attention. But the particular way she challenged assumptions of objectivity is what makes her a figure intriguing enough to merit her own biography. In her exposés of literary malpractice, she was unafraid to use some of the very manipulations she was decrying. The writs she issued to others were also blank checks made out to herself. Sneider’s subtitle, The Genius of Janet Malcolm , makes one fear a book of fangirl gush, probably the last thing Malcolm herself would have wanted. One flinches further upon learning that Malcolm had invited Sneider to tea after she, then still a Yale undergraduate, curated an exhibition of Malcolm’s papers in the university’s Beinecke Library. But seven years after that tea, Sneider, now a contributor to The New York Review of Books , has produced a book that assembles the biographical facts about Malcolm with admirable brevity, if not always precision. As for her subject’s writing, Sneider more or less concurs with a widespread verdict: “Malcolm acolytes will tell you that she is everywhere and nowhere within her work.” If traditional literary biography seeks to illuminate the work through the life, this one mostly reverses direction. The Absent Woman is a play on the title of Malcolm’s Plath book, and a kind of challenge that Sneider issues to herself and to readers: Go find the person in the books she wrote. Sneider’s voice is a lot breezier than Malcolm’s (whose isn’t?). The casual coarseness of her texting generation’s style (“pissing other people off,” “a little fucked up”) makes one imagine her blithely dropping crumbs on Malcolm’s carpet during that tea.

items.title: Lydia Millet’s Writerly Evolution Is All About Being More Shameless
items.summary: If you haven’t already read at least one of Lydia Millet’s books, the prospect might be daunting. By my count, there are 22 to choose from. Where to start? Do you go back to the madcap beginnings of her career and read the satirical George Bush, Dark Prince of Love ? Or do you look to Dinosaurs , a quiet meditation on ecology, community, and loneliness—a book that, for all the disaster it engages with, actually made me happier at the end than I was at the beginning? In true EL fashion, I have to say both, and. Millet has an astounding ability to write good book after good book after good book. Her concerns with human destruction, fallibility, consciousness, and the limits or limitlessness of our communication become ever more refined, ever more trenchant, ever more beautiful. One woman’s ceaseless interior dialogue, locked alone in a room in My Happy Life seems transmuted into the figure of a boy sleeping joyful and tentless in communion with the great outdoors in her latest book. It was a great pleasure to sit down and talk with Millet via Zoom in the run up to the publication of Fair Ones , a “double novel” that traverses romance, crime noir, coming-of-age, and honest to god social realism. There she was in her Walmart pavilion, nestled on the edge of a forest in Maine, reciting scraps of French poems she’d memorized in high school and holding forth on the importance of dancing even if it’s not pretty. The boundless energy it takes to write 22 books is on full display in our conversation. And if you’re still wondering where to start reading Millet after this interview, check out her many appearances in Recommended Reading — Willem Marx Associate Editor 1. What book should everyone read growing up? Lydia Millet: The Lorax . That’s a given though. It’s so obvious I shouldn’t even say it. I would also say the Narnia books. I adore them to this day. Or—it’s hard to just have one answer—Philip Pullman. His Dark Materials . 2. Write alone or in community? LM : Alone. When I was younger, I loved to write in coffee shops and bars. But I no longer do. Here in Maine, I sit in a hut, like a hundred dollar tent-pavilion thing from Walmart. We put it in the corner of our meadow, and I just sit out there. And in Arizona, I have a sort of guest house that belongs to my mother where I go and sit. So that’s my thing, outside and alone. It used to be bars, but I have no tolerance anymore. So what am I going to do at a bar? Just order water? I don’t think so. 3. Three presses that you’ll read anything from. LM: I’m not trying to be a kiss up, but I would honestly say Norton—which is obviously my own publisher. Once upon a time, I would have said Dalkey Archive. And Wave, which is poetry. That’s not to say that I love every book, but I will read every book and I will love many of them. 4. Hardcover, paperback, or e-reader ? LM: Opportunistic. I’ll read anything, but paperback is number one for me. Number two would be hardback, because I like paper better. But most frequently, I probably read on my tablet. I do all my library borrowing on the tablet because of distance and driving and all that stuff. So all the library books I read are digital. I love the digital library thing. I was always more of a library person. I’m not a collector. 5. If you were a novel, what novel would you be? LM: A Confederacy of Dunces ? [Laughs] No, no. I guess the closest would be one of my own books, truthfully. Probably Ghost Lights . The main character, Hal, is a guy who works for the IRS, and has discovered that his wife has been unfaithful. He’s quite a gentle, quiet person, which I’m not, but I think that I identify with that character most closely. What novel you would be is not the same as what character you would be, but that’s probably the closest I could come. I feel like comparing myself to someone else’s novel is arrogant. 6. Is there a genre you never want to write? LM: Romance. But also, you could go ultra specific, you know, those genres that are like quilting-pet-psychic-mysteries or something? Some really odd confabulation of genres. Self-help would be tough. Although I once wrote a book called Self Help when I was in college. It was terrible. Of course, the title was ironic. I wasn’t actually purporting to help others help themselves. When we were really young, my friends and I—a couple of friends who are also writers—used to fantasize about writing mass market fiction to make a quick buck. In particular, harlequin romances. Maybe it’s different now in the age of AI or in the age of cynicism or something, but I couldn’t write in some sort of weird gesture of mimicry or condescension or whatever. It’s actually quite hard to do that. Your heart’s gotta be in it in some way. 7. Describe your ideal writing day. LM: I’m fortunate because my ideal writing day is almost like the day I always have—if you take away the worries of life and things that happen, and there are many of those. But just in terms of its structure, it’s the day I get to have most often. I write for an hour and a half in the morning in a private place. And I do the same in the evening. Sort of in the cocktail hour before dinner. And that’s about it. That’s all I ask. And I do that every day I’m not dealing with a crisis or traveling or being sick. That wasn’t always the case. I used to just have to write during my workday, and I still have a 30-hour-a-week day job, but it’s sort of bracketed by those writing periods. I love my day job, but it doesn’t leave a lot of time for writing if you don’t have someone to help you with stuff like children and dogs and all that. I do have such a person now, so I’m fortunate to be able to write like that. It used to just be 15 minute snatches in between my day job until about 10 years ago. EL: What is your day job? LM: Since 1999, I’ve worked for the Center for Biological Diversity, which is a conservation and environmental organization. We do a lot of litigation for endangered species, climate change, and public lands. So a lot of scientists and lawyers that I work with every day. I’m like a language gatekeeper. I’m a copy editor and a general editor and I do some writing. I’ve done that 30 hours a week since my younger child was born, so almost 20 years. Wow, I had no idea. 8. Typing or longhand. LM: Typing. 100 percent. If I write longhand . . . I don’t even know. I’m just a mad woman, just completely insane. My brain is no longer calibrated to write longhand. I know writers who swear by it to this day, at least two of them. But I couldn’t. It would take a lot of work. If I were to be deprived of tech, it would take months and months of work, and then I would probably be a different writer. Not only in terms of measurable things, but qualitatively. It would be a different structure, a different idiom. EL: Did you always type? LM: No, I didn’t always type, although I always preferred it. As a teenager, I asked for a manual typewriter. I had this Olivetti. Then in college, I had a Tandy laptop. So I remember all these moments of having different things to type on over the years. But I also remember writing longhand while I was at jobs in my early 20s. Most of the writing I did longhand was playful. I didn’t write whole novels that way. 9. What’s a piece of writing advice you never want to hear again? LM: I mean, write what you know is the classic. Absolutely don’t write what you know, because you’ll be boring and you’ll never learn anything. Show don’t tell is another one. Of course, there’s a certain truth to all these. They’re meant to be reductive, but I actively disagree with them. It is accurate that you have to have the authority to tell something, and you have to produce that authority, and usually the best way to produce it i

items.title: When Your Debut Is Not Your First Book
items.summary: When I opened the Zoom, I was juggling feeding my toddler her yogurt pancakes and apologizing to Siang Lu for the chaos. We can reschedule, he said. I refused—just a few more bites and we’d be settled. He laughed and reminisced about the time his own children were that age, when he was trying to finish a book. “Which book,” I asked. “Your debut?” He smiled ruefully. His debut novel was The Whitewash , but the book he’d written first was actually Ghost Cities , which would go on to win the Miles Franklin Award, Australia’s highest literary honor. Back then, no one wanted it. This August, it finally gets its US debut. I first encountered Siang when he slid into my Instagram DMs to ask whether I’d let him include my debut novel in his long-running #sillybookstagram project, where he “defaces” book covers by inserting his own name. I didn’t know who he was, but the concept was so delightful that I readily agreed. Love Can’t Feed You became Siang Can’t Feed You . It was funny and, in that moment, I took the pain and gravity around my book’s reception less seriously. I knew immediately that someone with this kind of humor also carried serious intellectual weight, which is evident the moment you read his work. But what I didn’t realize until speaking to him is that his intellect and talent are only dwarfed by his great heart. Siang and I spoke candidly over Zoom and e-mail about failure, the publishing process, and what fatherhood does to an artist’s sense of time and purpose. Cherry Lou Sy: First, I want to say that I am part Chinese and when I encountered your character Xiang Lu, the translator who didn’t know a lot of Chinese and had to rely on Google Translate to the point of him being labeled #BadChinese, I thought, this is me. Siang Lu: Actually, putting that on the page was kind of exposing. It started out as a joke, but some people who read early versions of the manuscript really encouraged me to lean more into it, which was scary, because it’s something you’re sensitive about. But it has been a real joy—unexpectedly, at writers festivals and events—to have readers, not just Chinese but Indian, Pakistani, Greek, Italian, tell me that they are #BadChinese. That they relate to the second-gen migrant experience of not being fully educated in your own mother tongue and your own supposed culture, and what that means. I was born in Malaysia, ethnically Chinese, and I grew up in Australia having moved there from the age of four. Growing up in a Western culture, when you’re young, you tend to want to blend in. Anything that makes you different is actually quite painful. Consequently, you sort of just wish you were white. And it takes a really long time to deprogram from that. It wasn’t until I was almost 20 when I started realizing there was a way for me to embrace my culture. And eventually—this sounds like a paradox—I realized even without fluency in my mother tongue, there is a way nonetheless to be part of your culture and be a good ambassador for it. That was my attempt to write through it, write through that pain, and into something like acceptance. CS: You basically created your own version of “I am Spartacus.” That refrain—how many of us in the diaspora think of ourselves as #BadChinese? You might be a mature reader, but as a writer you’re just starting out. So you default to all of the same problems. SL: In Chinese and Malaysian culture, families are huge, so it was always the aunties and uncles who would bemusedly approach you at family gatherings and ask if you know how to speak the language yet. You end up memorizing a couple of phrases to get them off your back, which doesn’t really help anything. And it’s not only the self and the family—it’s also the media you consume. I think we’re in a different era now, which is good, and I’m glad my children are growing up in it. But when I was growing up, you wouldn’t see Asians on screen unless they were villains or ridiculous supporting characters. I was thinking about this recently: Why gravitate toward the page and toward fiction? I think it was a subconscious rejection of what I was seeing versus what I might be able to imagine for myself. Even though the stories I was consuming as a kid were just as problematic—I was still not seeing Chinese voices or culturally diverse voices—but it was somehow easier for me to find myself on the page. This is the part I was mulling on: the weird paradox of finding that medium, the blank imaginative slate. As you’re reading, you can picture everything—enough to have a toehold into this is my space, this is my place. As a reader, that’s comforting. But then you run into that problem again when you start writing, because suddenly you lack the maturity. You might be a mature reader, but as a writer you’re just starting out. So you default to all of the same problems. When I was starting out writing, I didn’t know how to center Asian stories. It was a difficult transition, trying to work through that love and finding myself on the page again. CS: I want to go back to the fact that Ghost Cities was actually your first novel, and The Whitewash was your second, but The Whitewash was the first to get published. That’s mind-blowing to me. SL: I’ve been writing since I was 19, and I’m 40 now. That’s entirely half my life, and the entirety of my adult life. It’s humbling how not good [of] a writer you can be for so long. Ghost Cities is actually the third book I wrote—the first two were so bad, and necessarily so, because I had the desire to write, the love of the form, the love of sentences, but I really didn’t know how to be me yet. I love to talk about failure. I’m so much less interested in success. I finished Ghost Cities in 2014, and it is not remarkably different from the version you’ve just read. There was a very long period where I was left alone with the idea that this thing I’d written, which I thought had value, nobody else agreed with. You’re dependent on external people to reflect back that the thing you’ve written is good. When you don’t have that, it becomes very difficult. But it’s also a nice lesson to learn: eventually, you’ll find your way into recognizing, okay, that thing was good. Maybe you’re being deluded—who knows—but you’ve got to come to that conclusion yourself. I had a US agent and we had a good run of submitting to US trade publications, and in the end we had to put it in the drawer. I thought forever. And just that long period of thinking about this, continuing to write—even that was a very deliberate decision, made after long periods of agonizing: Is it worth it? If no one’s going to read this, is it worth it? I hope other people don’t have to face that question, because it is very difficult. And I cheer on those success stories that come straight out of the gate. But we should also have stories like mine: that it is possible to endure far after the period when it seems appropriate to have given up. That was a strength for me. It allowed me to see who I was—which was a writer. I love to talk about failure. I’m so much less interested in success. But failure I could think about and talk about forever. And anytime I get off a stage having done so, just the amount of heartfelt conversations I’ll have with people from the audience. It makes me realize how necessary all of this is, and how probably we do not talk about it enough. We love to see the ready-made successes, especially in literature. But no one really talks about this long middle, and what it means to dedicate yourself to a practice and an industry that is fundamentally uncaring. items.title: Will the Hubble “constant” ever become an actual constant?
items.summary: It was nearly a full century ago that enough data came in to map out both the distance to a significant number of extragalactic objects and also measure the amount that their light was redshifted: interpreted as an apparent recession speed away from us. When the distance and recession velocity of those objects were plotted against one another, an intriguing relationship emerged: the farther away we looked, the faster an object seemed to be moving away from us. Twice as far meant twice as fast; ten times as far meant ten times as fast. This linear relationship became known as Hubble’s Law (or more recently, the Hubble-Lemaître Law, since Georges Lemaître derived it first), with the slope of that line known as the Hubble constant. However, it turns out that this is a complete misnomer: not only does the expansion rate of the Universe change with time, but it isn’t even constant across all of space right at this very moment. In other words, there’s nothing constant about the Hubble “constant” at all! The variation of the expansion rate with time was predicted from the star, but the variation in space came as a surprise: only with the discovery of dark energy did we realize this was the case. And yet, dark energy may turn out to be the Hubble constant’s ultimate savior, as if it truly is a cosmological constant, then one day, the Hubble parameter will, far into the future, actually become a constant after all. Here’s the science of what’s really going on. Hubble’s discovery of a Cepheid variable in the Andromeda galaxy, M31, opened up the Universe to us, giving us the observational evidence we needed for galaxies beyond the Milky Way and leading us, in short order, to the discovery of the expanding Universe. Credits : NASA, ESA and the Hubble Heritage Team (STScI/AURA); Illustration via NASA, ESA, and Z. Levay (STScI) Observationally, the story is seemingly straightforward. Beginning in the 1920s, our telescope technology became advanced enough — with large-enough aperture telescopes and the development of photographic plates — that we could start to resolve and identify individual stars in objects (i.e., galaxies) that were outside of our own Milky Way. The first such star was identified by Edwin Hubble in 1923: a Cepheid variable star, or a special class of star where, if you could measure the amount of time it took to brighten to its maximum, fainten to a minimum, and re-brighten back to its maximum again, you could know how intrinsically bright it was. Then, you could compare the observed brightness of that star (which you measured) with the intrinsic brightness that you just figured out, and that allows you to figure out the distance to it: the same way that, if you had a light bulb or candle with a known intrinsic brightness, then seeing how bright it appears would allow you to figure out how far away it is. This method for figuring out a distance in astronomy — the standard candle method — has since been extended to far more classes of objects than just Cepheid variable stars, and is one of the most useful tools in an observational astronomer’s arsenal. As was first noted by Vesto Slipher back in the 1910s, some of the objects we observe show the spectral signatures of absorption or emission of particular atoms, ions, or molecules, but with a systematic shift toward either the red or blue end of the light spectrum. When combined with distance measurements for those objects, this data gave rise to the initial idea of the expanding Universe: the farther away a galaxy is, the greater its light will appear redshifted to our eyes and instruments. Credit : Vesto Slipher, 1917, Proc. Amer. Phil. Soc. Then, in addition to figuring out the distance to that object, you can measure the light coming from that object as well. Rather than simply accumulating all the light of all different wavelengths together (a bolometric measurement ), or even by measuring the light across a variety of differently colored filters (a photometric measurement ), you could break that light up into all of its different component wavelengths, and measure the amount of light emitted at each specific wavelength along the way: a spectroscopic measurement . This technique, of spectroscopy, was the other key ingredient to uncovering the expanding Universe, and in turn, Hubble’s Law. When you break light up into its component wavelengths, you get to see an enormous number of features about it, including lines of two varieties: dark lines, known as absorption features, that occur at specific wavelengths and with specific intensities depending on the amount and density of any species of molecule, atom, or ion present, and bright lines, known as emission features, that occur at those same specific wavelengths that emerge from electrons transitioning between an excited state and a lower-energy state in molecules, atoms, or ions, at those same specific wavelengths. By comparing the observed wavelengths of (usually) absorption or (sometimes) emission features, we can determine an object’s redshift, and calculate the equivalent recession speed that corresponds to that redshift. Edwin Hubble’s original plot of galaxy distances, from 1929, versus redshift (left), establishing the expanding Universe, versus a more modern counterpart from approximately 70 years later (right). Many different classes of objects and measurements are used to determine the relationship between distance to an object and its apparent speed of recession that we infer from its light’s relative redshift with respect to us. As you can see, from the very nearby Universe (lower left) to distant locations over a billion light-years away (upper right), this very consistent redshift-distance relation continues to hold. Earlier versions of Hubble’s graph were composed by Georges Lemaître (1927) and Howard Robertson (1928), using Hubble’s preliminary data. Credit : E. Hubble; R. Kirshner, PNAS, 2004 Then, by plotting distance and redshift for the same sets of objects, together, we can make a graph for all sorts of extragalactic objects. This was done first by Georges Lemaître in an obscure 1927 paper (using much of Edwin Hubble’s data), then by Howard Robertson, independently, in 1928, and finally — and much more comprehensively — by Edwin Hubble himself in 1929. Although the points didn’t all lie exactly on a straight line, the overall trend was clear: the farther away an object was from us, on average, the greater its observed redshift, and hence, the greater its inferred recession velocity was. In all the time since those early measurements from the 1920s, throughout the early, mid, and late 20th century and even into the 1990s, we extended those measurements of distance and redshift to larger numbers of objects and evermore distant objects. Still, the slope of that best-fit line remained constant, and was named the Hubble constant. (In fact, the famed Hubble Space Telescope got its name because its primary mission was to pin down the measurement of that constant: the expansion rate of the Universe today.) Starting in the late 1990s, however, astronomers and astrophysicists made a shocking discovery. At the greatest of distances, the observed redshift-distance relation no longer followed a straight line, but instead departed from it. The theoretical implications of this — interpreted as evidence for the existence of dark energy — were astounding. This graph shows the 1550 supernovae that are a part of the Pantheon+ analysis, plotted as a function of magnitude versus redshift. The supernova data, for many decades now (ever since 1998), has pointed toward a Universe that expands in a particular fashion that requires something beyond matter, radiation, and/or spatial curvature: a new form of energy that drives the expansion, known as dark energy.
